jlbind lets an R package call Julia code without starting a separate Julia
session. It compiles Julia code into a shared library using
[JuliaC.jl](https://github.com/JuliaLang/Juliac.jl), then
exposes Julia functions to R through native `.Call()` routines.

This vignette explains how the shared library works and how to use an R package
built with jlbind. To add Julia functions to your own R package, see [Writing a
package that uses jlbind](writing-clients.html). For how jlbind compares with
other ways of calling Julia from R, see
[Performance](https://bjarkehautop.github.io/jlbind/articles/performance.html).

## How it works

An R process can load only one compiled Julia library. Julia has one runtime per
process, and that runtime uses a single compiled image. If two R packages loaded
separate copies of the library, they could conflict and crash the R session.

To avoid this, jlbind builds one shared library for each user, combining the
Julia bindings of all installed R packages that use jlbind. These packages are
called *clients*. Each client contains:

- A Julia binding package under `inst/julia/`, declaring the functions that R
  can call.
- A small generated C file that registers those functions as native routines.
- An `.onLoad()` hook that calls `jlbind::bind()` to connect the package to the
  shared library.

When you run `install_backend()`, jlbind finds the installed clients, compiles
their binding packages into one library, and saves it under
`tools::R_user_dir("jlbind", "data")`. When a client is loaded, `bind()` loads
the library if necessary and connects the client's native routines to it.

A client can only be bound to a library built from the version of that client
currently installed. If you update a package without rebuilding the library, its
functions will report that the library needs to be rebuilt.

## Using a package built on jlbind

You need [Julia](https://julialang.org/install/) 1.13 or later to build the
shared library.

After installing or updating an R package that uses jlbind, run:

```r
jlbind::install_backend()
```

The first build downloads and compiles the required Julia dependencies, so it
may take a few minutes. Because all clients share one library, installing or
updating a single client means rebuilding the library for all of them.

::: {.callout-note}
**Restart R after rebuilding a library that is already loaded**

Julia cannot be restarted within an R session. If the old library has already
been loaded, rebuilding it on disk does not replace the copy in memory. Restart
R to use the new library.
:::

### If something doesn't work correctly

If a package that uses jlbind doesn't work, first check its status:

```r
jlbind::check_backend("somepkg")
```

The most common causes are that the shared library hasn't been built yet, or
that the package was updated after the last build. Use `backend_info()` to
inspect the loaded library, the versions of the clients it was built from, and
which clients are currently bound.

If the Julia installation used for the build has been removed or replaced, for
example by a `juliaup` update, rebuild the library:

```r
jlbind::install_backend(force = TRUE)
```

You can select the Julia installation to use by setting the `JULIA` environment
variable or by passing `julia =` to `install_backend()`.

The library is compiled for the building machine's CPU. To use it on other
machines (e.g. cluster nodes), set `JULIA_CPU_TARGET=generic` and rebuild with
`force = TRUE`.

### Threads

Julia runs with one thread by default. To use multiple threads, set
`JULIA_NUM_THREADS` before loading the first package that uses jlbind. For
example, add the following to your `.Renviron` file:

```sh
JULIA_NUM_THREADS=auto
```

or

```sh
JULIA_NUM_THREADS=4
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Set the thread count before loading jlbind clients**

The thread count is fixed when the Julia library is loaded. Changing
`JULIA_NUM_THREADS` afterwards will not change the number of threads in the
current R session. Restart R after changing it.
:::

### Dependency versions

All clients share a single set of Julia dependencies, so they cannot each use
independent dependency environments.

By default, the build starts from the versions in the `Manifest.toml` [^1] of
the first client that has one, and keeps them for the other clients where their
`[compat]` bounds allow. Pass `update = TRUE` to use the newest versions every
client's `[compat]` allows instead.

[^1]: CRAN's [policy](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/policies.html)
    asks that external libraries downloaded at installation be a fixed version
    rather than the latest.

If a client's `[compat]` bounds conflict with those of the clients listed before
it by `jlbind_clients()`, it is left out of the build; `check_backend()` says
which clients it conflicts with.

You can control which clients are included by specifying them explicitly:

```r
jlbind::install_backend(packages = c("pkgA", "pkgC"))
```

Clients omitted from the build remain unbound until you rebuild the library with
them included.

::: {.callout-important}
**Clients with incompatible dependencies cannot share a library**

If you need both clients but never need them in the same R session, build a
separate library for each. Set `JLBIND_LIBRARY` before loading the client to
select the library for that session.

For example, build the two libraries:

```r
jlbind::build_library("pkgA", "~/jlbind/pkgA")
jlbind::build_library("pkgB", "~/jlbind/pkgB")
```

Then select one in an R session:

```r
# On Windows, use jlbind.dll; on macOS, use jlbind.dylib.
# On Linux, use jlbind.so.
Sys.setenv(JLBIND_LIBRARY = "~/jlbind/pkgA/jlbind.so")
library(pkgA)
```

Only one library can be loaded in an R session. In this example, `pkgA` is
bound, but `pkgB` is not.
:::
